June 29, 1966

to the attention of the government this sentence in their report:
Any suggestion that these older people, when the $75 pension is not sufficient, should be expected to depend for supplementation on public assistance after a needs test is utterly unacceptable.
This is what the Senate committee on aging has set forth, and it is in line with what has been the practice in this country with the old age security pension. Yet what the minister is proposing as the only solution for the senior citizens of this country is precisely this: To subject them to a needs test and then put them on social assistance.
I suggest that it is no answer for the minister to say that, no matter if they do have an increase in the old age security pension, they will still need the supplementary benefits under the Canada Assistance Plan. I will read what the Senate has to say on that, too, because after what we have seen today I do not want to leave out anything that is relevant:
Public assistance should, of course, be available to them,-
That is to the senior citizens.
*-as to others in the population, to meet residual needs and to deal with special circumstances, but it is the committee's conviction that main reliance for meeting their ordinary requirements should be on benefits to which they are entitled as a matter of right and that the proportion of older people requiring needs-tested supplementation should be very small at all times.
That is exactly what my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg .North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said last night, that if we needed the Canada Assistance Plan for those on old age security pension, it should be for those needs that are residual, whereas the minister is proposing to make the Canada Assistance Plan the actual supplement to their pension. In other words, he is proposing, after the old people have had this long hard fight waged for them to receive their pension as of right, instead of as charity, to pitchfork them into the ranks of the indigent, those people on social assistance, whom we are trying desperately to get out of that category. He is adding to the category of poverty the one category that had escaped to the dignity of the old age pension.
We say this is not good enough. The Senate committee on aging pointed out a way in which this problem could and should be solved. As a matter of fact the Senate committee suggested that we should have a guaranteed income for those on old age security pension. This has been rejected by the government. Perhaps the minister will tell me 23033-447
Canada Assistance Plan that it has not been rejected by the government, but we have been waiting to see it appear on the order paper this session. The old people are the population group in this country that cannot wait. The young ones may have some chance of survival if they can hang out long enough for enough pressure to be built up for the government to see the error of its ways, and come through to help them. But the old people cannot wait. That is why we have to look after their needs before we rise for the summer recess.
The Senate committee on aging proposed that we have a minimum income in this country and that we begin with the recipients of the old age security pension. I should like to ask the minister if he would be good enough to send me very soon the complete text of the speech he made at the opening of the welfare conference in Vancouver in the Queen Elizabeth theatre on June 20, because I have seen only the excerpts that he has sent around. I will swear on a stack of almost any book you care to provide that I heard the minister in that speech make reference to the desirability and need of exploring a guaranteed minimum income in this country.
I would very much like to find out whether it is in the text. I will not say categorically that he did say this, but unless my ears have gone back on me completely that is what he said in the speech. I remember that there was great applause at that point, because the welfare and social workers believe that the Senate is talking good sense when it suggests that we have a minimum guaranteed income for those on old age security in this country.
The government is evidently rejecting this proposal. I have heard government officials say, in private conversation at least, that a guaranteed minimum income would be too difficult to work out administratively. One of the most interesting addresses we had at the Canadian Welfare Conference in Vancouver was that of Professor Richard Titmuss of the London School of Economics. He told us that there is now going through the British House of Commons a piece of social security legislation which in its outlines is very like the guaranteed minimum income which has been proposed by the Senate committee on aging.
It is a piece of legislation under which they calculate the income of those people on social assistance, that of the old age pensioners and those in other categories of social need. They calculate the income of these people-incidentally, they do not take into consideration

June 29, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan the home in which they live-and take account of the taxes they have to pay. They permit an allowance whereby people can earn extra money, and then they calculate an allowance that people who are receiving various forms of state assistance, including pensions, are entitled to receive. At regular intervals a cheque is sent out to these people and at the end of the year they are asked whether their status has changed.
If their status has not changed, they continue to receive the cheque. What is the cheque? It is the difference between what these people are receiving and what the government considers to be a suitable guaranteed minimum income. That is the sort of thing we should be doing in Canada if our resources permit us to do it. If our resources do not permit us to do it, I suggest that the government take another look at its social priorities, because we ought to be able to cut expenditures in quite a few places and increase the pension received by our elderly people, those people who have built this country.
The minister spoke of the needs test enabling needs to be met with dignity and impartiality. Maybe they will be met with the impartiality that people show in meting out charity; but no dignity whatever is possible when assistance is received in the form of charity and not as of right. These old people have the right to receive what they have come to believe is their birthright, namely an adequate allowance without any questions being asked, an allowance as of right.
My criticism is not of the bill directly, so far as it goes. It is that nothing is provided, except what is in the bill, for senior citizens of this country. In my view this is what makes it absolutely necessary that we make one more try to achieve our purpose. If I could only describe what the older people in this country are up against I would give a great deal. I cannot do it. But I can read to the house two or three communications that I have received from Vancouver. I did not receive them last winter, or last week, but today. I have here a letter from the Federated Legislative Council of the Elder Citizens Associations of British Columbia in my own city of Vancouver, from which I quote the following:
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
We are aware of the fact that the Canada Pension Plan has nothing in it for those already retired; also that the suggested Canada Assistance Act
[Mrs. Maclnnis (Vaneouver-Kingsway) .1
holds little help for these people. We stress the need for immediate action in this regard because there are many who have already retired, and these are the people who need this now, not later.
We note that untold millions are being used for commissions of inquiry and increased government salaries in the higher brackets; also, that money is being sent overseas to eliminate poverty. At the same time many retired Canadians on a fixed income, founders of Canada, are actually in need.
Now I wish to read to you two communications which came to me this morning from people in my riding of Vaneouver-Kingsway. The first one reads as follows:
About pensions? What happened to Mr. Pearson's promise of $125 for the pensioners and help the poor program? Has it changed to pity the rich, the poor can beg? It looks like everybody won their raise in wages. The MP's and doctors just give themselves a raise without any argument. But the pensioner has to take what he gets and like it. Nearly all of them need a lot more to live on now. When the old age pensioners were growing up, wages were small and we did not have a chance to save much after paying taxes, raising families and putting children through school. Especially the ones that served in two world wars. You did not get very rich on $1.10 a day that we got in the first war. What is the government going to do about the high cost of low living? When the men get a raise it is for two or three years. But prices go up on everything every week through the year . . . Why should old age pensioners have to pay school taxes on top of other taxes when they have already paid to put their children through school? You won't get very fat off $75 per month after you pay your taxes, food, clothing, lights, gas, medical expenses, etc.
It happens my wife also has a pension and between us we get $1,800. In a country as rich as Canada $75 per month is a disgrace. Money paid in pensions is not wasted. It goes in circulation and makes more business. But money-millions of it is wasted making test planes and jeeps for army and air force-then the whole thing is junked . . . Something is wrong somewhere . . . With all the hundreds of millions to be spent on new construction across Canada, there must be a few extra dollars to help the pensioners catch up on the high cost of living.
I wish to suggest to you it is all very well to smile complacently or to think of going home for a holiday. These are flesh and blood people; they cannot eat averages. Other people may be making more on an average than they are, but it is our job to look after them.
Here is another letter which I will read to you. It says:
I am 84 years old and since last January when I got a heart stroke I was still working parttime as an expert gardener, a hobby of mine that I made my trade when I was laid off at the Canadian White Pine at 66. Having raised four children at that time, I had $50 in the bank, no debts and my little house paid for. I had to wait four years for the $40 pension at that time and my wife is seven years younger than I am. Still we have managed and made some saving.
June 29, 1966

These are not indigents or social assistance cases. These are people who have been robbed through no fault of their own by the continuous increase in the cost of living. The letter goes on to say:
When I was 70 I inquired if I may get the health insurance only, but I was told that X will be obliged to take the pension also and stop working, so I turned it down and fortunately that medicare came just handy a few months before my stroke. All these personal details are only to help you to state the case of many thousands who are penalized for working hard and being thrifty and I have a few thousand dollars savings at the bank that will take care of us to the end, but it is a matter of principle and justice.
I know the actual game just as well as yourself. The raise of the pension to $100 is fully justified and imperative right now for one-third of the pensioners in the low bracket and will cost $100 million. There exists at this time a real majority for it . . . They use the bogey of inflation and wait their own sweet time at the next election two or three years from now to buy enough votes by raising the pension to everybody and it is well known that no inflation ever occurs before an election-it is only after.
I will now suggest to you that people of this calibre, people who have been self-respecting, self-sustaining and thrifty, do not merit the humiliation and indignity of being dumped back into a means or a needs test. These are the people to whom we should give something very much better at this time.
I offer no apologies for taking the time of the house tonight because this is one of the purposes for which I came down here. This is one of the reasons for which I was sent down from Vancouver-Kingsway. The people there feel they have been getting the short end of the stick, and there are a great many old age pensioners at that short end. The very least we can do is to give them $100 a month at the age of 65 without requiring a means test.
The old age pensioners are the most defenceless of all people and the ones who have the least time to waste. We remember that it was a Liberal government who once before waited too long and then gave too little and too late. We saw the same sort of death-bed repentance exercised in Prince Edward Island by the Conservative government, or shall we call it the former government, I do not know which. This again was a case of too little and too late. We have been fighting for this measure for a long time and I do not aspire to a halo in calling for immediate action to be taken. It is part of our belief that those people who were the pioneers of this country should be able to live in dignity and peace until the end of their days. We cannot agree to adjourning parliament until something is 23033-447*
Canada Assistance Plan done for them. We are now preparing to celebrate Canada's 99th birthday with pomp, ceremony, fanfare and a brand new flag while the pensioners, some of whom have also reached the age of 99, suffer hunger, penury and loss of dignity.
Let me say emphatically that death-bed repentance is better than no repentance at all. We have still a few hours left before recessing and if the government wishes the house to wait so that they can draft legislation in respect of old age pensioners, let me tell them every party in this house will cheerfully wait for such legislation. I also wish to suggest that although death-bed repentance may not get you into heaven, it might save you quite a long term in purgatory.

Mr. Speaker, half a century ago George Bernard Shaw wrote:
The evil that must be fought is not sin, suffering, greed, it is neither monopolization, ignorance, alchoholism, war, nor plague, it is simply poverty.
Needless to say then that the bill under consideration is much to my liking. Even though it is not complete and does not meet all our wishes, I feel it will bring to the people something they need. Mr. Speaker, in listening to the speech of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin), for whom I have the greatest admiration, I felt that perhaps he should have subtitled it, "Never look a gift horse in the mouth". I think that the particular gift horse called the Canada Assistance Plan needs considerable examination, and the longer one looks at it the more disturbing this kind of legislation becomes. Many of the reasons for the dissatisfaction with this legislation have been indicated by my colleagues and by members of other parties, although the plan has some advantages.
I was interested to see how the plan would be applied and would affect those people who are currently having difficulties and require assistance. Like all members of parliament I get letters asking for assistance which perhaps comes within the provincial field. Like all members of parliament who find it difficult to make excuses or to appear to be passing the buck, I get involved in these matters and I am given the opportunity of seeing some of the cases that come before provincial governments and some of the problems with which they have to deal.
This morning I went through my files and took out just a few of the letters that have come to my attention in order to make an analysis of these problems, based on my personal experience, to see in just what way the Canada Assistance Plan is going to be of help and whether it is the best way of providing assistance to those people who require help. A very interesting fact arises from an examination of these letters, and I suggest to all hon. members on the government side that they take a look at the letters they have received to see whether their experience is not similar to mine. I should like

to read some of the letters I have received and perhaps draw some conclusions from the problems outlined in these letters as to what is the best approach to the personal problems of many of the people of this country.
The first one begins in this way:
I am writing this letter to let you know I am now 66 years old. On September 9 I will be 67 years old and we get the old age pension for one-
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
This family, Mr. Speaker, needs assistance very badly. I am not going into all the details of the letter. The husband's asthma is very bad and he will be in hospital. The key phrase in the letter is "66 years old". The implication of this and of many other letters I have received-and I will be repeating this point over and over again-is that if there were an old age pension of $100 a month at age 65 much of the problem evidenced in this letter will disappear. There is no need for provincial assistance here. There is no need for a needs test or a means test or anything else. This situation can be dealt with effectively by means of an adequate old age pension. Another letter says:
I wonder if you can intercede to get me a little more old age pension as I am finding it very hard to keep up with doctor bills and the drugs which are needed. Also, we have to keep up our home as well.
Here again, an increased old age pension would solve this difficulty. Medicare, which we are now awaiting, would take care of another aspect of this situation. Thus, two programs within the jurisdiction of the federal government would be sufficient to meet the needs in this field.
I could go on to show that in letter after letter the key words, drugs, sickness, illness, old age, keep appearing. Yet the government is proposing that we accept a short-term measure designed to fill in the interstices of a welfare program and adopt it as a solution to welfare needs.
Either the government does not understand the nature of what is happening or else it refuses to face realities. It is my opinion that a great many of the welfare cases now being handled by the provinces would disappear if adequate old age pensions were paid and a suitable medicare program introduced. If we have a choice in this country, and I believe we do, why do we propose legislation of the kind before us when legislation of he kind to which I have referred is obviously called for? It is true there will probably always be a need for supplementary
June 29, 1966

legislation in this field to deal with cases which do not fall within general categories, but surely we should not be asked to enact legislation such as this when the need for an increase in old age pensions throughout the country is so obvious.
Like many other members of the house I am concerned about the prestige of parliament. I am concerned about the loyalty of the people of Canada to their federal government. The other night I listened with interest to an amendment proposed by an hon. member on the government side and supported by the hon. member for St. John's West as a means by which government prestige might be improved. The method suggested was that we should write into all legislation providing federal assistance to the provinces a provision to the effect that a sign must be put up giving the federal government due credit for its share of the assistance and indicating the degree to which the federal government had participated.
I said then that this seemed to show a far greater concern for public relations than for doing things which would genuinely merit the affection of the people of Canada. This kind of thing is symptomatic of the legislation before us.
I say to members on the government side that they are taking a long step toward abdicating their responsibility in the field of old age assistance, and the vacuum they create by this abdication will be filled by the provinces themselves. Hon. members opposite may rest assured of that. The province of Prince Edward Island has already indicated that it recognizes the importance of making available a minimum of $100 a month to old age pensioners and intends to provide a supplement. Does the minister believe that other provinces will not take similar action? Does he not realize that such provinces will probably find a way of getting the federal government to pay a large portion of the cost in any event? Is he prepared to let a responsibility of this kind pass from his into other hands because he is unwilling to use his authority and unwilling to make a decision?
I presume that should the provinces decide to make supplementary payments to old age pensioners they could go to the federal government under the terms of the legislation before us and obtain financial assistance with respect to the supplementary payments on the basis of the percentage of the people covered. Thus the cost would be borne to a considerable extent by the federal government.
Canada Assistance Plan
The result will be that the people will look on the federal government and say: What fools they are. Why did they let this come to pass? Naturally they will be grateful for assistance, whether it comes from the federal government or the provinces. But they will see one further indication that the federal government is refusing to act in the face of an evident need.
If supplements are paid, and I cannot see how it can be avoided any longer, the money will have to be found one way or another, either within the limits of provincial taxation or in the area of federal taxation. Surely the federal government has far better instruments for taxation at its disposal than have the provinces. If this tax is to be raised at the provincial level, the tendency will be for it to come from the home owners or from the smaller people of this country.
I was interested in the emphasis placed upon the distinction between means and needs. On the surface there seemed to be a concern to explain that the needs of certain individuals would be met to a greater extent under this legislation than was possible in the past and that the old means test might be changed. Certainly the hope was expressed that the attitude toward it might be changed. But the minister gives no indication of recognizing there is any occasion for a needs test as between one province of Canada and another. Here we have a program which says in effect: If you are a wealthy province and can raise large sums of money we shall give you large sums of money but if you are a poor province, unable to raise as much, we shall only give you an amount matching whatever you can raise.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Is this the best the minister could have done, especially when he knows full well the disadvantages afflicting some areas? Could a better formula not have been devised? Is it right that a poor province should be treated no differently than a rich province? Is this the way we are going to help correct the inequities that exist? Is this not a program to freeze the status quo? It appears that that is what the legislation is designed to do, and for that reason it falls far short of what is required in present circumstances.
Sometimes the question is asked, "How are we going to pay for it"? All kinds of suggestions are made in this regard, but the impression left by government spokesmen is that we cannot afford it. Yet the record indicates that Canada, one of the wealthiest nations in the

June 29, 196S
Canada Assistance Plan western world, a nation with a standard of living second only to the United States, spends less on social welfare as a percentage of gross national product than nations much poorer.
I wish to read from a United Nations study published in 1961. Some changes have taken place since that time, mainly because of the introduction of the Canada Pension Plan, which will change the figures slightly, but the statistics in the report are startling. It shows the proportion of social welfare expenditures to gross national product in various countries. The percentages exclude education but include health, family allowances, social security and public assistance of various kinds. In the United Kingdom the figure is 11 per cent, in Sweden 10.5 per cent, in West Germany 9.4 per cent, in Australia 9.1 per cent, in France 5.8 per cent and in Canada 5.7 per cent. Our percentage is not pleasant to contemplate.
An earlier study by the International Labour Organization in Geneva, made from a different viewpoint and published under the title "The Cost of Social Security, 1949-1954", arrived at the following comparative percentages of gross national product: West Germany 19.2 per cent, France 18.5 per cent, Italy 14.7 per cent, Sweden 11.5 per cent, United Kingdom 10.7 per cent, Netherlands 9.6 per cent and Canada 9.1 per cent. On the basis of those figures I do not think anyone can say that this country has been overly generous in taking care of the social welfare needs of its citizens.
Last year I was proud to be a member of the parliament which passed the Canada Pension Plan. We in this party gave that plan our wholehearted endorsement because we realized the great value of that type of program. We have always supported, if not even sponsored, the old age security program, and we are on our way now toward building up a good comprehensive social security program provided the government does not backslide as it is doing with respect to this legislation and by not increasing the old age pension.
Once the old age security program reaches a certain level the government will have to consider seriously the need for an income related program such as suggested by the Senate committee on aging. If the government does the right thing with regard to the old age security program, the right thing being to increase the pension to $100 per month at age 65, if it uses the Canada

Assistance Plan in the way it should be used, as a supplement to take care of those instances that do not fall within the broad general cetegory, and if it then acts on the Senate committee report, the minister and the government will have reason to be proud instead of being under the gun as they have been for the last few days so far as this particular problem is concerned.
The minister has seen how deep is the feeling of members on this side of the house and I am sure he has been made aware of the depth of feeling among members of his own party about the need to increase the old age pension. He really cannot ignore this expressed feeling any longer. Quite frankly, I do not understand what he is waiting for because surely he must realize that he has to do something about old age security and that he has to raise the pension.
If the minister does not raise the old age pension, then the provinces will. Is the minister prepared to abdicate his responsibility, to sit back and say: The federal government is timid; if the provinces want to do it that is their business and we will help them out? Does he honestly believe that the Canada Assistance Plan will help the great number of older people who need assistance, taking into account the pittance he is providing under the plan for a nation of 20 million people, a pittance that is supposed to do so many things?
Helping older people is only one aspect of this program. There are all kinds of things that this program is designed to do. Can the minister stretch $80 million that far? Surely he knows he cannot, and surely he knows our older people cannot live on $75 per month. When the minister replies I hope he will say he has listened to those voices from every political party, including his own, who have pleaded with him to do something for our older people.
Everything has been done that I believe is possible to do. We have had pleas to the minister's good nature. We have had threats to defeat the government. We have had threats to sit here all summer if need be. But up to the present moment the minister has retained great equanimity in the face of all these things. If these things do not move him and he says he needs a better reason to be moved, let him search his own heart, examine the situation of our older people and then stand up and tell the house that his government is prepared to do something worth while before we adjourn this summer.

Mr. Speaker, I have hesitated to inject myself into this debate because I am myself concerned. Approaching as I do in a month or two the end of my 70th year, naturally I am personally involved to some extent. However, I think it is perhaps time that someone of my generation should speak on behalf of the vast number of people in Canada who have reached my age or a greater age and are left in the situation in which they have been left today by this and previous governments.
There are several ways by which the degree of civilization of a people may be measured. We may measure it perhaps by the number of cars that block our highways. We may measure it perhaps by the measure of ostentation with which a nation proceeds to celebrate its 100th birthday. We may measure it by the number of millionaires we have. There are numerous ways. But I suggest a more valid measure of the degree of civilization of any people is the manner in which they treat and consider those at both ends of life's scale.
What is important is the way we approach the situation of the more vulnerable and more helpless members of our community. I may tell you that even one such as myself who looks forward to retirement without any particular misgivings on that score, knowing I shall be comfortable enough in my last days, realizes that as one gets old one is obliged to recognize the fact that one becomes more and more vulnerable, more and more helpless and more and more dependent on the compassion, generosity and kindness of one's fellow human beings.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that it is a terrible indictment of the degree of civilization of the people of Canada for this government to refuse to move in this manner to give relief to those who are in the age group to which I belong and those who are older. It seems quite shocking to me that Canadian people who have never known hunger, who have never known despair and who have never known misery and poverty should, in the midst of a society which we think of as being the second most affluent in the world, be content to leave hundreds of thousands of their fellow citizens in a condition of misery.
I think of the old lady in my constituency who I met casually a few weeks ago who was obliged to subsist on a diet of corn flakes for
Canada Assistance Plan the last two weeks of the month before her cheque came in. She seemed rather surprised when I expressed my shock. She said: "Oh, there are many like me; some take shredded wheat but I take corn flakes and survive until the next cheque comes in." She was rather philosophical. She thought it was rather shocking that she had been left in this condition because she had worked hard all her life, but she assumed that eventually parliament would get around to providing an income which would produce something more than corn flakes in the last week of the month.
I know we shall be told repeatedly as we have been told in the past that we cannot afford this. I know that in the editorial columns of every financial page in this country we will be warned that we must go carefully and that we cannot move too fast in the direction of the welfare state.
I know we will be asked where will the money come from. There are a number of places we could suggest. I am going to suggest one. I would suggest that if we were prepared to cut in half the hundreds of millions of dollars we have thrown down the drain, ever since I first entered this house 13 years ago, on so-called defence, we could easily care for the needs of the old people of this country. I have not heard one minister of national defence in all that time-and I have sat opposite a succession of them-tell us that with this vast expenditure of funds the security of the Canadian people has been in any way ensured. This is a prestige thing, and there is no other reason for it. Anyone who examines the situation knows perfectly well that Canada cannot make any meaningful contribution toward the military strength of the western world. But for prestige purposes we continue to throw the money away and say we cannot afford to look after our own people. That is a scandalous scale of values.
I was reminded of this the other day while speaking to a representative of one of the small Caribbean nations. I asked him whether his people had an army. He said: "Oh, no, we cannot afford an army." Then he turned to me and smiled and said: "Anyway, I would hope we would have too much sense to pretend that we could afford one." The inference was perfectly obvious. He considered we did not have as much sense as he hoped his people would have.
In my part of the country in the early days the native population on Vancouver Island

June 29, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan solved the problems of the old people perfectly simply. They had a simple method. When an old man or an old woman was unable any longer to contribute to the work and welfare of the tribe he or she was taken out to the ocean at low tide and parked there with a small package of food. The tribe then went back to the land and waited for nature to take its course. We are not quite as kind as that, because we insist on giving our old people a little money so that the tides of poverty will not sweep them away immediately and they will have plenty of time in their later years to repent the fact that they spent their lives working for the benefit of the community and Canada and trusted us to see that they would be looked after in their old age.
I would suggest that if one wishes to advance an argument there is no better argument than this to convince the government, and it seems that one has to adduce these arguments to get any action from this dilapidated and discredited government. Let no one doubt that it is dilapidated and discredited. If it is seeking some operation which will be a face-lifting operation, there is no better place to do it than to do it here by bringing in legislation which will not solve the problems of the old people of the country and will not enable them to live in luxury but which, by adding merely $25 a month, perhaps will relieve some of the poverty, misery and frustration under which they live today.
I know quite well that if the government does this it will be subjected to criticism, as I said earlier, in every financial paper in the country. It would be subjected to criticism on every editorial page in the country because the people who write these things represent those who do not wish to have further expenditures placed on them in order that the old people will be helped. It will take a certain amount of courage, I quite admit, for the government to fly in the face of these newspaper editorial writers and financial critics.
Courage unfortunately has been one quality which has been in conspicuously short supply in this government. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if this government hopes to save itself then this is about the only card it has left to play. It should summon its courage and play it now today and not later when it will be revealed to the people of Canada that it has been forced to do something which it did not have the courage and decency to do on its own initiative.

This is a slow process. During the last 40 years we have experienced a change in public opinion with regard to social security. It was frowned upon in early days when people were supposed to work and save. I remember very early in life, at the age of 10, 11 and 12, walking behind my father on the day before Christmas and pulling my toboggan or sleigh laden with parcels to distribute to needy families, and at that early age I saw the crippling effects of poverty.
One family which I had to look after, not only at Christmas time but during the year, kept on increasing year by year until it got to the size of two adults and 13 junior members. Even as a small boy I rather wondered how the head of that family, who had nothing but a minor job as a caretaker, could raise such an enormous brood, but it has taken us a long time to realize that it is not possible for everybody in this country to earn a satisfactory living and save for their old age. As the years have gone by we have discovered that this is an impossibility for a great many people and that the state has an obligation on their behalf.
The wealth of a nation rests with its people, in addition to its natural resources. Unless its people are strong and healthy and have a good outlook on life, the nation suffers accordingly. I know all about the depression years. I saw their evil effects on hundreds of people. I saw their effect on a class of 40 high school boys, aged 17 and 18, whose fathers had been unemployed for anywhere from one to five years.
During the last year I was engaged in teaching those boys were not interested in school. They would have been drop-outs had

there had been any place to drop to. But strangely enough, a year later when the war broke out these young men at age 17, 18 and 19 put on their country's uniform and served in the navy, army or air force. Three of them became officers in the Canadian Army; yet they had been making no progress in school. At the time I knew them in 1938 all these lads were headed for the unemployment line, just like their fathers, to live on the dole and eke out an existence. But when the time of crisis came they served their country. They served their country well and several of them lost their lives.
It is no advantage to our country to have thousands of children living under meagre conditions. It is no advantage to us if we have 200,000 needy mothers with dependant children eking out a bare existence. These are the present and future adult citizens of our country. They deserve sufficient food to develop healthy bodies and sufficient stimulus through education of the mind so that they will be useful citizens. The mothers of these needy children should be not be ground down by toil and worry and end up in ill health. The psychological effect is, of course, even greater if a family can see no sign of life but just a grim existence stretching ahead from day to day.
It is no credit to a country to fail to give its senior citizens that which they deserve. They deserve something beyond a mere existence, and over the years we have fortunately reached a stage where our senior citizens are getting much better attention than they got some years ago.
I recall visiting senior citizens in the city of Winnipeg 20 years ago. I particularly remember three elderly men in their eighties, eking out an existence on an old age pension of $30 a month and living in squalid quarters. I asked how they managed to keep alive and how they got their food. They told me that on Monday morning they went to one of the stores and bought stale bread left over from Saturday. They were boiling a cup of tea when I visited them and I asked how much the gas cost for the ring they were using. They replied, "We are pretty smart. You watch that kettle. The minute it begins to hum we switch the gas off, the water comes to a boil from the heat still left in the ring and then we make our cup of tea." The only tobacco they had was what was given to them.

It is my intention to say a few words only because the longer I sit in this house and listen to the responses of the government and the minister to questions put to them by members on this side as to why they will not increase the old age pension, the more I am convinced that they have given no adequate reason why this should not be done.
I should like to ask the minister to explain precisely why the government will not do something to alleviate the low income problem facing the elderly people of our country. There is adequate information at our fingertips which shows quite clearly that the absolute minimum level of income needed by old age pensioners today is somewhere in the order of $110 to $140 a month. The amount varies in the various studies that have been conducted. For example, I have before me a summary of information which emanated from the Canadian Conference on Aging.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
It is their estimate that the absolute minimum required by an old age pensioner to allow him to live the way we want him to live is $138.96 per month. The Toronto Metro Social Planning Council has estimated that $126.47 per month is the absolute minimum necessary for old age pensioners. Other studies have also been conducted in this regard. It should be obvious to hon. members on the government side that it has been adequately proved there is need for an increase in the purchasing power of our older citizens and an increase in old age pensions.
I think this is the right time to ask the minister-I am not doing this in a taunting manner as it is not my desire to taunt hon. members opposite-in view of the data collected and the studies carried out on the level of income necessary for old age pensioners, how in the world the government can sit back and allow the pension to remain at $75 a month. This amount is about 50 to 65 per cent below the level regarded as an absolute minimum by the various study groups which have looked into the matter.
It has been argued by hon. members opposite, and particularly by the minister when presenting this legislation, that it will serve to provide additional income to those people who, upon a means-needs test analysis, prove that they are eligible for it. However, surely the minister should not be so anxious to provide this additional income by means of

such a complicated and involved means-needs test system. Why enter into the thicket of red tape when it can be done with ample justification and in a much simpler way by means of a universal increase of old age pensions to $100 a month?
I am sure hon. members opposite, including the minister, may from time to time take the view that some members on this side of the house are exploiting this issue for partisan or political gain. Nevertheless I suggest to the minister that if he holds this opinion it is a very harsh one indeed. If hon. members opposite indulge in name calling and suggestions as to who is or is not hypocritical-I am now referring specifically to the charge made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) that a member of our group was being hypocritical when speaking of the need for increasing old age pensions-then I point out to the minister that we on this side can indulge in the use of precisely the same kind of language.
We have been made aware of the publicity which the government has given in recent months to the war on poverty and we consider it to be hypocritical in the light of the government's attitude to the level of old age pensions today. If the government really intends to deal with the problem of poverty immediately and with the minimum amount of red tape, it can do so forthwith in the area involving old age pensioners.
Is the government refusing to adopt the request of hon. members on this side? Is the government refusing to increase old age pensions because this country cannot afford it? Is that the answer they are giving us, or are they refusing to increase old age pensions at the present time because it might have an adverse effect on the economy resulting in inflation? Is that the government's reason for not increasing old age pensions? If this is so then I will put to the minister what I consider to be a rather more obvious answer. If, in the opinion of the minister, this country cannot afford to increase pensions to $100 a month, then the government is applying a strange set of priorities because we are spending much larger amounts of money in other sectors of the economy which have nothing to do with ordinary humanitarianism and common decency toward our old people.
If that is the reason which the minister wishes to give us, then I suggest that if our purchasing power must somehow be decreased or inhibited so as to dampen demand

it is very strange that it is our older people who are chosen to bear this burden first. In so far as old age pensions are concerned, I should like to make a specific reference to the effect of this legislation on the elderly people in rural areas. I know from personal experience that during the past 15 years the incomes of most Canadian farmers have been much below the hoped-for level. In fact, it has been readily admitted by successive ministers of agriculture that income in the Canadian agricultural industry has been a serious problem in that the costs of farmers have been increasing and the prices they have been receiving for their commodities have been remaining static or in some cases have even declined. This has had an effect on those farm people who have come to their retirement years recently and, because they have had low net incomes over the past decade, are facing a very bleak retirement. Until such time as the Canada Pension Plan takes full effect, which is still almost a decade away, these people have little to hope for in the way of enhanced retirement pensions. Is it really asking too much of the

June 29, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan government or the minister to consider this specific aspect of the problem of universal old age pensions?
In my opinion it is partly the fault of the Canadian government that net farm income has been low over the past decade. Since it has been partly the fault of the government, it seems to me there is an onus upon the government to take some tangible, concrete step to alleviate the problem facing these farm folk who are coming to retirement age in the immediate future. I know the Canada Assistance Plan will be of some help in this regard. However, there will be this complicated, protracted means-needs test type of investigation. Many farm folk find this very awkward because a computation must be made of their net assets. The value of their old machinery must be computed and the value of the land and old buildings. This is really an administrative nightmare for a social worker or anyone taking applications for old age assistance in these farm areas and trying to determine whether or not these people have the means to meet their needs.
So, Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude on this note. While the Canada Assistance Plan now before us is perhaps in some ways a distinct improvement over the situation which has existed, nevertheless in one important respect it is a very real disappointment. While it may succeed in providing certain improvements in our social assistance programs, it nevertheless imposes this means-needs test-I use the two words conjointly- on the many elderly people of our country. I dare say the country could well afford, and should want to afford, just a little bit better. The cost of living index has shown a substantial increase in recent months. Yet there has been no indication from the government what they intend to do about adjusting the universal old age pension to accommodate this increase. I hope the minister will not be so intransigent in this regard that he will simply not consider the request for some legislation to be introduced within a relatively short time to give our old age pensioners a level of income which at least approaches the income levels described as absolutely necessary by such organizations as the Toronto Metro Social Planning Conference, the Canadian Conference for the Aged and so on.
As a new member of the house I am actually astounded when I watch the government stubbornly refuse to admit that the present old age pension level is simply unacceptably low in the light of the cost of living. I

am astounded that the government has not been moved so far to take any tangible, direct action to deal with this matter. There is no point in my saying any more, Mr. Speaker, for the simple reason that if the government cannot be persuaded in a few words, with complete absence of taunting, complete absence of acrimony, then it is not likely they will be persuaded at all.

Their future at the moment seems bleak and without much hope unless they wish to go through a complicated, and in my opinion unnecessary, means-needs test. The minister should make amends before he is condemned by the elderly people of this country.
